units.title: Sounds, letters and the alphabet
goals: Read any Spanish word aloud from its spelling, because Spanish spelling records pronunciation closely
Know every letter of the alphabet, including 'ñ', its name as said in Mexico, and the sound or sounds it stands for
Say the five vowels without gliding, and tell diphthongs from vowels in separate syllables
Apply the rules that choose a consonant's sound in Mexican Spanish ('c', 'z' and 's'; 'g', 'gu', 'gü' and 'j'; 'qu'; 'h' and 'ch'; 'll' and 'y'; 'r' and 'rr'; 'b' and 'v'; 'd'; 'x'; 'tl')
Spell your name aloud and recognize the signs '¿', '¡', the acute accent and the dieresis
grammar: The alphabet: 27 letters including 'ñ', their names in Mexico ('be grande', 've chica', 'doble u', 'i griega'), and the digraphs 'ch', 'll', 'rr', 'qu' and 'gu'
The five vowels, always pure and never weakened; strong and weak vowels; diphthongs, and 'y' as a vowel in 'hoy' and 'muy'
Seseo: 'c' before 'e' or 'i', 'z' and 's' all sound [s] in Mexico; 'c', 'qu' and 'k' for [k]; 'g', 'gu', 'gü' and 'j'
The letters 'b' and 'v' as one sound; softer 'b', 'd' and 'g' between vowels; the tap 'r' and the trilled 'rr'; silent 'h'; 'll' and 'y' as one sound; 'ñ'
The letter 'x' as [ks] in most words and [x] in 'México' and 'Oaxaca', 'tl' in words from Nahuatl, and the written signs '¿', '¡', the acute accent and the dieresis
vocabulary_themes: words chosen only to illustrate each sound or spelling rule
letter names and spelling your own name aloud
pairs told apart by one sound ('pero' and 'perro') and pairs that sound alike in Mexico ('casa' and 'caza')

units.title: Stress, accent marks and punctuation
goals: Divide a word into syllables, find the stressed syllable, and know the terms 'aguda', 'grave' and 'esdrújula'
Apply the default stress rule and decide whether a word needs a written accent
Explain why 'café', 'lápiz', 'teléfono', 'día', 'país', 'tú' and 'qué' carry an accent mark, and why 'examen' has none while its plural 'exámenes' does
Tell apart words spelled alike by the accent mark ('tú' and 'tu', 'sí' and 'si', 'él' and 'el', 'qué' and 'que')
Write questions and exclamations with '¿' and '¡', and use capital letters as Spanish does
grammar: Syllables and how to divide them; diphthongs, triphthongs and vowels in hiatus; the stressed syllable

The default rule: words ending in a vowel, 'n' or 's' are stressed on the second to last syllable and all others on the last; a written accent marks every word that breaks the rule and every word stressed on the third to last syllable
The accent on a stressed 'i' or 'u' beside 'a', 'e' or 'o' ('día', 'país', 'baúl'), which keeps the two vowels in separate syllables

The accent that tells apart two words spelled alike ('tú' and 'tu', 'él' and 'el', 'mí' and 'mi', 'sí' and 'si', 'sé' and 'se', 'té' and 'te', 'dé' and 'de', 'más' and 'mas'), and the accent on question and exclamation words
Accents that appear and disappear in plurals and feminines ('canción', 'canciones'; 'joven', 'jóvenes'; 'inglés', 'inglesa'); the 2010 spelling rules ('solo', 'este', 'guion'); capitals; '¿' and '¡'
vocabulary_themes: words that show each stress pattern and each reason for an accent
pairs of words told apart only by an accent mark
the words of the previous unit, now with their stress explained

units.title: How Spanish works: the big picture
goals: Name the parts of speech and the terms of grammar used in this course (subject, object, infinitive, conjugation, person, number, tense, mood, agreement, gender) in English and in Spanish
Explain how a Spanish sentence is built and where it differs from English: adjectives after the noun, no helper verb 'do', 'no' before the verb and a subject that is often left out
Predict the gender of most nouns from their endings, form plurals, and make articles and adjectives agree with the noun
Explain how a verb is built from a stem and an ending that shows who acts, and know the map of tenses and moods the course teaches
Choose between 'tú', 'usted' and 'ustedes' for 'you', and use the two contractions 'al' and 'del'
grammar: Word order: subject, verb, object; adjectives usually after the noun; no helper verb for questions or negation; 'no' before the verb and the double negative ('no ... nada')
Nouns have gender and number; the definite articles 'el', 'la', 'los', 'las' and the indefinite 'un', 'una', 'unos', 'unas'; agreement of articles and adjectives
Verbs: the infinitive ('-ar', '-er', '-ir'), stem plus ending, conjugation by person and number, the dropped subject, and the map of tenses and moods
Subject pronouns and the forms of address used in Mexico ('tú', 'usted', 'ustedes'), and why 'usted' and 'ustedes' take the verb forms of 'él' and 'ellos'
Prepositions and the two compulsory contractions ('a' and 'el' give 'al', 'de' and 'el' give 'del'); a first look at 'ser', 'estar', 'tener' and 'ir'
vocabulary_themes: the names of the parts of speech in English and Spanish
the small function words used in every sentence ('el', 'la', 'un', 'una', 'de', 'en', 'a', 'y', 'que', 'no')

units.title: Greetings and introductions
goals: Greet people at different times of day and say goodbye
Introduce yourself, ask someone's name and say that you are pleased to meet them, with 'tú' and with 'usted'
Say where you are from and what nationality you are
Use the present tense of 'ser' with the subject pronouns
Use the basic courtesy expressions, including the Mexican reply '¿mande?', and say what each one literally means
grammar: Present tense of 'ser' ('soy', 'eres', 'es', 'somos', 'son') and when the subject pronoun is said
'Ser de' for origin; nationalities and their agreement ('mexicano', 'mexicana'; 'canadiense'; 'estadounidense')
Fixed formulas and what they literally say: 'buenos días', '¿qué tal?', 'mucho gusto', 'encantado' and 'encantada', '¿cómo te llamas?' and '¿cómo se llama?', '¿mande?'
Forms of address: 'señor', 'señora', 'señorita' and 'joven' for strangers, and 'don' and 'doña' before the first name of a respected older person, all used with 'usted'
vocabulary_themes: name, origin and forms of address ('señor', 'señora', 'don', 'doña')

units.title: Ser, estar and how you feel
goals: Ask and answer '¿Cómo estás?' and '¿Cómo está usted?'
Describe people with adjectives that agree in gender and number
Choose between 'ser' and 'estar' in simple cases
Say what someone does for a living, and make sentences negative with 'no'
Ask questions with 'quién', 'cómo', 'dónde', 'qué' and 'por qué', and answer with 'porque'
grammar: Present tense of 'estar' ('estoy', 'estás', 'está', 'estamos', 'están')
'Ser' for identity, origin, profession and lasting traits; 'estar' for location, conditions and feelings
Adjective agreement in gender and number, including adjectives ending in '-e' or a consonant
Professions with 'ser' and no article ('Soy maestra'); negation with 'no'; question words and their accent; 'por qué' and 'porque'

units.title: Numbers, age, time and dates
goals: Count from 0 to 100 and give a phone number
Say your age, and say that you are hungry, thirsty or sleepy, with 'tener'
Tell the time and ask when something happens
Say the days of the week, the months and the date
grammar: Numbers 0 to 100, the accent in 'dieciséis', 'veintidós', 'veintitrés' and 'veintiséis', and 'veintiún' and 'un' before a masculine noun
Present tense of 'tener' and its use for age ('tengo treinta años') and for states ('tener hambre', 'tener sed', 'tener sueño', 'tener frío', 'tener calor')

Telling time: '¿Qué hora es?', 'Es la una', 'Son las dos', 'y media', 'y cuarto', 'cuarto para las tres', the form used in Mexico for a quarter to three, 'de la mañana', 'de la tarde', 'de la noche', 'a las tres'
Days and months as masculine nouns written in lowercase; 'el lunes' for 'on Monday'; dates with 'el primero' and cardinal numbers ('el cinco de mayo')
vocabulary_themes: days of the week and months
time-of-day words ('la mañana', 'la tarde', 'la noche', 'el mediodía')

units.title: Family, articles and possessives
goals: Talk about your family and your friends
Use definite and indefinite articles correctly
Form the plurals that change their spelling or accent ('los lápices', 'las canciones') and the plurals that do not change ('los lunes')
Say whose something is with possessive words and with 'de'
grammar: Definite and indefinite articles and their uses, including 'el' before a feminine noun that begins with a stressed 'a' sound ('el agua')
Plurals: '-s', '-es', 'z' becoming 'c' ('el lápiz', 'los lápices'), and accents that appear or disappear
Possessives 'mi', 'tu', 'su', 'nuestro' with their plurals and feminine forms; the many meanings of 'su' and 'de él', 'de ella' and 'de usted' to make 'su' clear
'De' for possession ('el carro de Ana', 'la casa del maestro'); '¿de quién?'; the masculine plural for mixed groups ('los papás', 'los hermanos')

units.title: Food, drinks and ordering
goals: Order at a taquería, a café and a restaurant
Say what you want and what you prefer
Talk about meals and what there is to eat
Ask for the bill and leave a tip
grammar: Regular present tense of '-ar' ('hablar'), '-er' ('comer') and '-ir' ('vivir') verbs
Stem-changing verbs, first pattern: 'querer' and 'preferir' change 'e' to 'ie' in stressed syllables ('quiero', but 'queremos')
'Hay' for what exists ('Hay tacos'), with no article for an unspecified amount ('Quiero agua'); 'un poco de', 'más', 'otro'
Ordering formulas: 'quiero', '¿me da...?', '¿me trae...?', the polite form 'quisiera', 'para llevar', 'para aquí', 'la cuenta, por favor'
vocabulary_themes: Mexican everyday food ('los tacos', 'las tortillas', 'los frijoles', 'el chile')

units.title: Likes, dislikes and free time
goals: Say what you like and dislike with 'gustar' and 'encantar'
Ask other people what they like, with 'tú' and with 'usted'
Agree and disagree with 'a mí también', 'a mí tampoco', 'a mí sí' and 'a mí no'
Talk about hobbies and how you spend your free time
grammar: 'Gustar': the thing liked is the subject and the person is an indirect object ('me gusta el café', 'me gustan los tacos'); 'gusta' with an infinitive
The indirect object pronouns 'me', 'te', 'le', 'nos', 'les' in this construction, and 'a mí', 'a ti', 'a usted', 'a él', 'a Ana' for emphasis or clarity
'Encantar' and 'interesar', which work like 'gustar'; 'no me gusta nada'
Agreeing and disagreeing: 'a mí también', 'a mí tampoco', 'a mí sí', 'a mí no'

units.title: Daily routine
goals: Describe a typical day
Ask about someone's routine
Say how often you do things
Say at what time and in what order you do things
grammar: Reflexive verbs and the pronouns 'me', 'te', 'se', 'nos', placed before the conjugated verb ('me levanto', 'se baña'), which explains 'me llamo'
Stem-changing verbs: 'o' to 'ue' ('poder', 'dormir', 'acostarse'), 'e' to 'i' ('pedir', 'vestirse'), 'u' to 'ue' in 'jugar', and 'e' to 'ie' recycled ('despertarse')
Verbs with an irregular form for 'yo': 'hacer' ('hago'), 'salir' ('salgo'), 'poner' ('pongo'), 'ver' ('veo')
Frequency and time: 'siempre', 'casi siempre', 'a veces', 'nunca', 'todos los días'; 'en la mañana' and 'por la mañana'; 'temprano' and 'tarde'

units.title: Places and directions
goals: Name places in a Mexican town
Ask for and give directions
Say where things are with 'estar' and where you are going with 'ir a'
Say whether you know a fact with 'saber' and a place or a person with 'conocer'
grammar: Present tense of 'ir'; 'ir a' and the contraction 'al'; '¿adónde?'
'Estar' for location and the prepositions of place 'cerca de', 'lejos de', 'al lado de', 'enfrente de', 'detrás de', 'entre', 'en la esquina'; 'aquí', 'ahí' and 'allá'
'Saber' ('sé') for facts and 'conocer' ('conozco') for places and people; the preposition 'a' before a person who is a direct object ('Conozco a Diego')
Directions with fixed command forms: 'siga derecho', 'dé vuelta a la derecha', 'camine dos cuadras', taught as phrases
vocabulary_themes: places in town ('el centro', 'la plaza', 'el mercado', 'la farmacia', 'el museo')
directions ('la cuadra', 'la esquina', 'a la derecha', 'a la izquierda', 'derecho')
getting around on foot and by car

units.title: Shopping, colors and prices
goals: Ask for prices and sizes
Describe clothes and their colors
Point things out with 'este', 'ese' and 'aquel'
Pay in pesos, in cash or by card, and bargain politely at a market
grammar: Demonstratives 'este', 'ese' and 'aquel' with their feminine and plural forms, and the neuter forms 'esto', 'eso', 'aquello'
Numbers from 100 to 1,000,000 ('cien' and 'ciento', 'quinientos', agreement in 'doscientas'); pesos and centavos; years
Colors: agreement, colors with one form for both genders ('azul', 'verde'), position after the noun, '¿de qué color?'
'¿Cuánto cuesta?' and '¿cuánto es?'; 'qué' and 'cuál' for choices; 'quedar' like 'gustar' for fit ('me queda grande'); exclamations with 'qué' ('¡Qué caro!')
vocabulary_themes: payment ('la tarjeta', 'en efectivo') and the street market ('el tianguis')

units.title: Home and housing
goals: Describe your home
Say what there is in a place with 'hay' and where a thing is with 'estar'
Ask about renting an apartment, 'un departamento'
Say which floor something is on
grammar: 'Hay' for what exists versus 'estar' for where a known thing is ('Hay un sofá en la sala'; 'El sofá está en la sala')
'Muy' versus 'mucho'; 'mucho', 'poco', 'bastante' and 'demasiado' as adjectives that agree and as adverbs that do not
Location words 'arriba', 'abajo', 'adentro' and 'afuera'; 'vivir en'
Ordinal numbers 'primero' to 'décimo', with 'primer' and 'tercer' before a masculine noun ('el primer piso')

units.title: Plans, weather and invitations
goals: Talk about future plans with 'ir a' plus an infinitive
Describe the weather and the rainy season
Invite someone, and accept or decline politely
Say what you can, want, need and have to do
grammar: The near future: 'ir a' plus an infinitive ('Voy a viajar mañana')
Verbs followed by an infinitive ('poder', 'querer', 'pensar', 'necesitar', 'deber'), and 'tener que' plus an infinitive
Weather: 'hace calor', 'hace frío', 'hace sol', 'llueve', 'está nublado', 'el clima'
Invitations: '¿Quieres...?', '¿Vamos a...?', '¿Qué tal si...?', '¿Te late?'; accepting and declining ('claro', 'lo siento, no puedo', 'me encantaría, pero...'); 'ahora', 'ahorita' and 'al rato'
vocabulary_themes: time words for the near future

units.title: A1 consolidation
goals: Combine A1 skills in longer conversations
Introduce yourself in detail
Handle a café, a shop, directions and small talk
Ask for help when you do not understand
Review the key grammar of A1
grammar: Review: address, 'ser', 'estar', 'tener', 'ir', 'hay', regular, stem-changing and reflexive verbs in the present, 'gustar', 'ir a' plus an infinitive
Common beginner errors: 'ser' versus 'estar', 'hay' versus 'estar', gender agreement, 'gusta' versus 'gustan', the preposition 'a' before a person as direct object
'Algo', 'nada', 'alguien', 'nadie', 'alguno' and 'ninguno', with the double negative
Connecting sentences with 'y', 'pero', 'porque', 'entonces' and 'o', and 'y' becoming 'e' and 'o' becoming 'u' before the same vowel sound
vocabulary_themes: survival phrases ('no entiendo', '¿cómo se dice...?', '¿qué significa...?')

units.title: The past: regular preterite
goals: Say what you did yesterday and last weekend
Ask questions about past events
Use past time markers, including 'hace' plus a length of time
Spell the forms for 'yo' that change their spelling ('busqué', 'llegué', 'empecé')
grammar: The preterite of regular '-ar', '-er' and '-ir' verbs, all persons, and why 'hablé' and 'habló' carry an accent
'Hablamos' and 'vivimos' as both present and preterite
Spelling changes in the form for 'yo' ('busqué', 'llegué', 'empecé') and the 'y' of 'leyó' and 'creyeron'
Time markers: 'ayer', 'anoche', 'anteayer', 'la semana pasada', 'el año pasado', 'hace dos días'; the Mexican preterite with 'ya' ('¿Ya comiste?')

units.title: The past: irregular preterite
goals: Use the most common irregular preterite forms
Tell a short story in order
Talk about a trip or an event
grammar: 'Ser' and 'ir' share 'fui', 'fue', 'fuimos', 'fueron'; 'dar' ('di', 'dio') and 'ver' ('vi', 'vio') with no accent

Preterites with a new stem and unstressed endings: 'tener' ('tuve'), 'estar' ('estuve'), 'poder' ('pude'), 'poner' ('puse'), 'saber' ('supe'), 'hacer' ('hice', 'hizo'), 'querer' ('quise'), 'venir' ('vine'), 'decir' ('dije', 'dijeron'), 'traer' ('traje')
Stem changes of '-ir' verbs in the preterite: 'pedir' ('pidió'), 'dormir' ('durmió'), 'divertirse' ('se divirtió')
Sequencing words: 'primero', 'luego', 'después', 'por fin'
The present of 'venir', 'decir', 'traer', 'dar' and 'oír' ('vengo', 'digo', 'traigo', 'doy', 'oigo')

units.title: The imperfect: habits and descriptions
goals: Talk about your childhood and past habits
Describe past scenes, people and states
Say what you used to do with 'soler' and the imperfect
grammar: The imperfect: '-aba' for '-ar' verbs and '-ía' for '-er' and '-ir' verbs, and why 'comía' and 'hablábamos' carry an accent
The three irregular imperfects: 'ser' ('era'), 'ir' ('iba'), 'ver' ('veía'); 'había' as the past of 'hay'
Uses: habits, descriptions, background, age, time and weather in the past ('Eran las ocho', 'Tenía diez años')
'Soler' plus an infinitive ('solía jugar'); 'siempre', 'antes' and 'cuando' with the imperfect

units.title: Preterite versus imperfect
goals: Choose between the two past tenses
Tell a story with a background and events
Say what was going on when something happened
grammar: Event versus background, and an action interrupted by another ('Leía cuando sonó el teléfono')
Verbs that change meaning: 'conocí' and 'conocía', 'supe' and 'sabía', 'quise', 'no quise' and 'quería', 'pude' and 'podía', 'tuve que' and 'tenía que'
Narrative structure: setting, trigger, result
Connectors: 'mientras', 'cuando', 'de repente', 'en ese momento'

units.title: Direct object pronouns
goals: Tell a direct object from a subject
Replace a direct object with 'lo', 'la', 'los' or 'las'
Place object pronouns before a conjugated verb or after an infinitive
Use the neuter pronoun 'lo' in 'no lo sé' and the fixed expression 'pasarla bien'
grammar: The direct object and the pronouns 'me', 'te', 'lo', 'la', 'nos', 'los', 'las'; 'lo' and 'la' for 'usted'; Mexican usage of 'lo' for a man
Placement: before a conjugated verb ('lo veo'), attached to an infinitive ('voy a verlo') or before the whole phrase ('lo voy a ver'); 'no' before the pronoun
The neuter pronoun 'lo' for an idea ('No lo sé', 'Ya lo sé') and fixed expressions with 'la' ('pasarla bien')
A direct object placed first and repeated by a pronoun ('El pastel lo compré yo')

units.title: Indirect objects and double pronouns
goals: Tell an indirect object from a direct object
Use 'le' and 'les', together with the noun they refer to ('Le di el libro a Ana')
Combine two object pronouns, with 'le' becoming 'se' ('Se lo di')
Use the pronouns that follow a preposition ('para mí', 'conmigo', 'contigo')
grammar: Indirect object pronouns 'me', 'te', 'le', 'nos', 'les' beyond 'gustar', and the normal doubling with 'a' plus a noun ('Le dije a Diego')
Two pronouns together: the indirect before the direct ('me lo', 'te la'), and 'le' and 'les' becoming 'se' before 'lo', 'la', 'los', 'las'
Pronouns attached to an infinitive and the accent the longer word needs ('dármelo', 'dárselo')
Pronouns after prepositions: 'mí', 'ti', 'usted', 'él', 'ella'; 'conmigo' and 'contigo'

units.title: Work, jobs and the progressive
goals: Talk about your job and workplace
Say what is happening right now
Handle a simple phone call
Say what was going on at a moment in the past
grammar: 'Estar' plus the gerund ('-ando', '-iendo'); irregular gerunds ('leyendo', 'yendo', 'durmiendo', 'diciendo', 'pidiendo')
Present versus progressive: the progressive only for an action in progress, never for a planned future
Pronouns with the gerund ('lo estoy haciendo', 'estoy haciéndolo') and the accent the longer word needs
'Estaba' plus the gerund for an action in progress in the past; 'seguir' plus the gerund; 'todavía'
vocabulary_themes: phone phrases ('¿bueno?', '¿de parte de quién?', 'un momento')

units.title: Instructions and commands
goals: Give and follow instructions with 'tú', 'usted' and 'ustedes'
Read and write a simple recipe
Make requests and prohibitions
Place object pronouns correctly with commands
grammar: Affirmative 'tú' commands: the form of the present for 'usted', 'él' and 'ella' ('habla', 'come'), and the eight short irregulars 'di', 'haz', 've', 'pon', 'sal', 'sé', 'ten', 'ven'

Commands for 'usted' and 'ustedes' and every negative command use present subjunctive forms, built on the form for 'yo' with the opposite vowel ('hable', 'coma', 'no hables'), with spelling changes ('busque', 'llegue', 'empiece') and the irregulars 'sea', 'vaya', 'dé', 'esté', 'sepa'
Pronouns attached to affirmative commands and placed before negative ones ('dímelo', 'no me lo digas'), with the accent the longer word needs
Softer requests ('¿Me pasas...?', '¿Puedes...?') and the infinitive on signs ('No fumar')
vocabulary_themes: a Mexican salsa and other recipes
kitchen tools and ingredients ('la olla', 'el jitomate', 'la cebolla')

units.title: Health and the body
goals: Name the parts of the body
Describe symptoms at a doctor's office or a pharmacy
Understand and give simple medical advice
Say what hurts
grammar: 'Doler' like 'gustar' ('me duele la cabeza', 'me duelen los pies'), with the definite article for body parts
'Tener' plus a noun for symptoms ('tengo fiebre', 'tengo tos', 'tengo gripa'); 'sentirse' ('me siento mal')
Advice: 'tener que', 'deber' and 'hay que' plus an infinitive; commands for 'usted' from the doctor ('tome', 'descanse', 'no coma')
Reflexive verbs with body parts ('me lavo las manos', 'se rompió el brazo')
vocabulary_themes: illnesses and symptoms ('la gripa', 'la fiebre', 'la tos')
the doctor's office and the pharmacy

units.title: Travel, transport, por and para
goals: Buy tickets and book a room
Get around by bus, metro, car and plane in Mexico
Ask about departures, arrivals and travel times
Choose between 'por' and 'para'
grammar: 'Para' for destination, purpose, recipient and deadline; 'por' for cause, route, exchange, duration and means ('por la mañana', 'por teléfono', 'gracias por')
Transport with 'en' ('en camión', 'en metro', 'en avión') and 'a pie'
Schedules: 'sale a las', 'llega a las', '¿cuánto tarda?'
Polite requests with the fixed forms 'quisiera' and 'me gustaría', whose tenses come later
vocabulary_themes: the bus terminal and the airport ('la central de autobuses', 'el boleto', 'la maleta')

units.title: Comparing things and people
goals: Compare two things, people or actions
Say that something is the best, the most or the least
Express equality and difference
Compare belongings with 'el mío' and 'el tuyo'
grammar: 'Más' or 'menos' plus an adjective plus 'que'; 'más de' before a number; 'tan ... como' and 'tanto ... como'
Irregular comparatives 'mejor' and 'peor' (from 'bueno' and 'malo'), 'mayor' and 'menor'; superlatives 'el más ... de'; '-ísimo' and its spelling changes ('riquísimo')
Possessive pronouns 'el mío', 'la tuya', 'los suyos', 'las nuestras', and the same forms after a noun ('un amigo mío')
Adverbs in '-mente' built on the feminine adjective ('rápidamente'), and comparing actions ('más rápido', 'mejor')

units.title: The future and the conditional
goals: Talk about the future with the simple future and with 'ir a'
Make polite requests and suggestions with the conditional
Guess about the present with the future of probability
Talk about goals and dreams
grammar: The simple future: the infinitive plus '-é', '-ás', '-á', '-emos', '-án', and the irregular stems ('tendr-', 'saldr-', 'pondr-', 'vendr-', 'podr-', 'sabr-', 'querr-', 'har-', 'dir-', 'habr-'); 'ir a' plus an infinitive as the everyday future in Mexico
The conditional: the infinitive plus '-ía', with the same irregular stems; politeness with '¿Podría...?', 'me gustaría', 'debería'
The future of probability ('¿Qué hora será?', 'Estará en su casa')
Suggestions: '¿Por qué no...?' and 'yo que tú'

units.title: A2 consolidation
goals: Tell a story using both past tenses
Write a short email or message
Handle longer everyday conversations, including a complaint
Review the key structures of A2
grammar: Review: preterite, imperfect, object pronouns, progressive, commands, 'por' and 'para', comparisons, future and conditional
Connectors: 'pero', 'además', 'sin embargo', 'por eso', 'así que', 'pues', and 'aunque' with the indicative
Common A2 errors: preterite versus imperfect, the order of two pronouns and 'se lo', 'por' versus 'para'
Writing short messages and emails: openings and closings ('Saludos', 'Un abrazo')

units.title: The present perfect and participles
goals: Form and use the present perfect
Form regular and irregular participles
Talk about experiences with 'alguna vez' and 'nunca'
Know when Mexican speakers use the preterite instead of the present perfect
grammar: 'Haber' in the present ('he', 'has', 'ha', 'hemos', 'han') plus the participle ('-ado', '-ido'), which never agrees and is never separated from 'haber'
Irregular participles ('hecho', 'dicho', 'visto', 'escrito', 'abierto', 'puesto', 'vuelto', 'roto', 'muerto', 'resuelto', 'descubierto') and the accent in 'leído', 'oído', 'traído'
Mexican usage: the present perfect for experiences and for situations that continue to now; the preterite for completed actions, even today ('¿Ya comiste?')
'Acabar de' plus an infinitive; participles as adjectives with 'estar' ('la tienda está cerrada')

units.title: The present subjunctive: wishes and requests
goals: Explain what the subjunctive mood is and why Spanish needs it
Form the present subjunctive of regular, stem-changing, spelling-change and irregular verbs
Express wishes and requests with 'querer que', 'pedir que', 'esperar que' and 'ojalá'
Choose between an infinitive (same subject) and 'que' plus the subjunctive (different subject)
grammar: The subjunctive as the mood that does not assert; the clause and the conjunction 'que'

Formation from the form for 'yo' with the opposite vowel; stem changes, including '-ir' verbs in the form for 'nosotros' ('pidamos', 'durmamos'); spelling changes; the irregulars 'ser', 'estar', 'ir', 'dar', 'saber', 'haber'; the form for 'nosotros' as 'let's' ('hablemos', 'vámonos')
Triggers of will and influence: 'querer que', 'esperar que', 'pedir que', 'necesitar que', 'preferir que', 'recomendar que', 'decir que' for a command; 'ojalá', an interjection
Same subject (infinitive) versus different subject ('que' plus subjunctive); good wishes ('que te vaya bien', 'que te mejores')

units.title: The subjunctive: emotion, doubt and judgment
goals: React to events with verbs of emotion
Express doubt and denial
Make judgments with impersonal expressions such as 'es importante que'
Contrast 'creo que' with 'no creo que'
grammar: Emotion: 'me alegra que', 'me molesta que', 'me preocupa que', 'me sorprende que', where the clause with 'que' is the subject of a verb that works like 'gustar'; 'tener miedo de que'
Doubt and denial with the subjunctive ('dudar que', 'no creer que', 'no es cierto que') versus certainty with the indicative ('creer que', 'estar seguro de que', 'es verdad que')
Impersonal expressions ('es importante', 'es necesario', 'es posible', 'es mejor', 'es una lástima') with 'que' plus the subjunctive, or with an infinitive when no one is named
'Quizás' and 'tal vez' with either mood, and 'a lo mejor', common in Mexico, with the indicative

units.title: The subjunctive with time, purpose and condition
goals: Talk about future events with 'cuando' plus the subjunctive
Express purpose with 'para que'
Set conditions with 'en caso de que', 'a menos que' and 'con tal de que'
Contrast these with the indicative and the infinitive
grammar: Time conjunctions with the subjunctive for an event that has not happened ('cuando llegues', 'en cuanto', 'hasta que', 'después de que', 'tan pronto como') and with the indicative for habits and past facts
'Antes de que' always with the subjunctive; 'antes de', 'para' and 'sin' plus an infinitive when the subject is the same; 'al' plus an infinitive ('al llegar')
Purpose and condition: 'para que', 'sin que', 'a menos que', 'con tal de que', 'en caso de que'
'Aunque' with the indicative for a fact and with the subjunctive for a possibility
vocabulary_themes: plans that depend on other people

units.title: Relative clauses
goals: Build longer sentences with relative pronouns
Put a preposition before a relative pronoun
Use 'lo que' and 'lo' plus an adjective
Use the subjunctive when the person or thing described is unknown or does not exist
grammar: 'Que' for people and things; 'quien' after a preposition and between commas; 'donde'
A preposition plus an article plus 'que' ('la amiga con la que hablé'); 'el cual' and 'la cual'; 'cuyo', which agrees with the thing possessed
'Lo que' ('lo que quiero') and 'lo' plus an adjective ('lo bueno', 'lo mejor es que')
Indicative versus subjunctive in relative clauses ('Busco un departamento que tenga jardín'; 'No hay nadie que sepa')
vocabulary_themes: describing people and places in detail

units.title: The imperfect subjunctive and hypotheticals
goals: Form the imperfect subjunctive from the preterite
Talk about unreal situations with 'si' plus the imperfect subjunctive and the conditional
Report past wishes and requests ('Quería que vinieras')
Use 'ojalá' and 'como si' with the imperfect subjunctive
grammar: Formation from the preterite form for 'ellos': 'hablaron' gives 'hablara', 'tuvieron' gives 'tuviera', 'fueron' gives 'fuera'; the accent in the form for 'nosotros' ('habláramos'); the '-se' forms recognized as a written alternative
'Si' plus the imperfect subjunctive plus the conditional ('Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría más') versus 'si' plus the present for real conditions
Sequence of tenses: a past main verb with the imperfect subjunctive ('Me pidió que lo ayudara'); 'quisiera' explained
'Ojalá' plus the imperfect subjunctive for unlikely wishes; 'como si' plus the imperfect subjunctive

units.title: Passive and impersonal constructions
goals: Use the passive with 'ser' plus a participle
Use 'se' for passive and impersonal sentences ('Se venden casas', 'Aquí se come bien')
Read signs, ads and announcements
Tell 'estar' plus a participle for a result from 'ser' plus a participle for an action
grammar: The passive with 'ser' plus a participle plus 'por', with agreement ('La ciudad fue fundada por los mexicas'), mostly in writing, news and history
The passive use of 'se' with agreement ('se vende casa', 'se venden casas') and the impersonal use of 'se' with no subject ('se trabaja mucho', 'se busca a dos meseros')
'Estar' plus a participle for a resulting state versus 'ser' plus a participle for the action
Impersonal third person plural ('Dicen que va a llover') and 'uno' and 'tú' used impersonally

units.title: Pronominal verbs, change and unplanned events
goals: Tell 'ir' from 'irse' and other pairs whose meaning changes with 'se'
Describe changes with 'ponerse', 'volverse', 'hacerse' and 'quedarse'
Talk about accidents and unplanned events with 'se me olvidó' and 'se le cayó'
Use 'se' and 'nos' for actions that two people do to each other
grammar: Verbs whose meaning changes with 'se': 'ir' and 'irse', 'dormir' and 'dormirse', 'quedar' and 'quedarse', 'llevar' and 'llevarse', 'parecer' and 'parecerse'
Verbs of becoming: 'ponerse' (a passing change), 'volverse' (a change of character), 'hacerse' (through effort or time), 'quedarse' (a resulting state)
The pronoun 'se' of unplanned events with an indirect object ('Se me olvidaron las llaves', 'Se le rompió el vaso'), where the thing is the subject
Reciprocal 'se' and 'nos' ('se conocieron', 'nos vemos') and the order of 'se' with other pronouns

units.title: Starting, stopping and continuing
goals: Say that an action starts, stops, happens again or continues
Say how long something has been going on with 'llevar' plus a gerund and 'hace ... que'
Use 'volver a', 'dejar de', 'ponerse a' and 'estar a punto de'
Talk about habits and resolutions
grammar: The verbal periphrasis: a conjugated helper verb plus an infinitive, a gerund or a participle with one meaning; 'ir a', 'tener que', 'acabar de' and 'estar' plus a gerund recycled
Starting and stopping: 'empezar a', 'ponerse a', 'dejar de', 'terminar de', 'volver a', 'estar a punto de'
Duration: 'llevar' plus a length of time plus a gerund ('Llevo dos años estudiando español'), 'hace' plus a length of time plus 'que', 'desde hace', 'seguir' plus a gerund
'Andar' plus a gerund in Mexican speech ('ando buscando trabajo') and 'deber de' plus an infinitive for a supposition

units.title: Work, paperwork and formal register
goals: Write a formal email
Handle a job interview
Deal with documents and government offices in Mexico
Switch between formal and informal registers
grammar: Formal register in writing: 'usted' throughout, 'su' and 'le' for the reader, 'Estimado' and 'Estimada', 'Atentamente', the Mexican closing 'Quedo a sus órdenes'
Request formulas: 'Le escribo para', 'Me gustaría solicitar', '¿Podría indicarme...?', 'Le agradecería que' plus the imperfect subjunctive
Formal register in speech: 'usted' with strangers, older people and officials; professional titles as forms of address ('licenciado', 'ingeniero')
Polite refusals and reported requests ('Me pidieron que trajera...')
vocabulary_themes: documents ('la credencial', 'el acta de nacimiento', 'el comprobante de domicilio')
government offices and paperwork ('el trámite', 'la ventanilla')

units.title: Opinions, news and debate
goals: State and defend an opinion
Agree and disagree politely
Discuss news and current topics
Summarize what someone says
grammar: Opinion expressions: 'en mi opinión', 'creo que', 'para mí', 'me parece que', 'estoy de acuerdo', 'no estoy de acuerdo'
Hedging and softening: 'hasta cierto punto', 'en cierto modo', 'por lo menos', 'la verdad es que'
A first look at reported speech in the present: 'dice que', 'pregunta si', 'pide que' plus the subjunctive
Review of the subjunctive versus the indicative in argument ('No creo que sea justo'; 'Creo que es justo')
vocabulary_themes: social topics ('la seguridad', 'la educación', 'el medio ambiente')

units.title: The pluperfect and the other compound tenses
goals: Use the pluperfect for an action before another past action
Form and use the future perfect and the conditional perfect
Form and use the perfect and pluperfect subjunctive
Talk about regrets and unreal past conditions
grammar: The pluperfect ('había hecho') for an action before another past action
The future perfect ('habré terminado') for completion and for probability; the conditional perfect ('habría ido')
The perfect subjunctive ('haya llegado') and the pluperfect subjunctive ('hubiera sabido'); 'Si hubiera sabido, habría ido' and the colloquial Mexican pattern 'Si hubiera sabido, hubiera ido'
'Ojalá' plus the pluperfect subjunctive for regret; 'deber haber' plus a participle

units.title: Reported speech
goals: Report statements, questions and commands
Shift tenses and references when the report is in the past
Summarize a conversation or an interview accurately
grammar: Tense shifts after a past reporting verb: present to imperfect, preterite to pluperfect, future to conditional, present subjunctive to imperfect subjunctive, a command to 'que' plus the subjunctive ('Me dijo que viniera')
Reporting verbs: 'afirmar', 'asegurar', 'negar', 'advertir', 'reconocer', 'comentar', 'aclarar', 'mencionar'
Indirect questions with 'si' and with accented question words ('Me preguntó dónde vivía'); changes of time and place ('hoy' to 'ese día', 'aquí' to 'allí', 'mañana' to 'al día siguiente')
Reports without a tense shift when the fact still holds ('Me dijo que viene mañana'); the repeated question with 'que' ('¿Que si vienes?')

units.title: The subjunctive: concession and nuance
goals: Use concessive structures with the right mood
Use the subjunctive with 'el hecho de que', in repeated-verb phrases and after indefinites
Choose the mood that changes a sentence's meaning
Follow the sequence of tenses across all the subjunctive tenses
grammar: Concession: 'aunque', 'por más que', 'por mucho que', 'a pesar de que', 'si bien', with the indicative or the subjunctive by meaning
Repeated-verb phrases and indefinites: 'pase lo que pase', 'digan lo que digan', 'sea como sea', 'cualquiera que sea', 'dondequiera que', 'como quieras'
'El hecho de que' and a clause with 'que' at the start of a sentence with the subjunctive ('Que no venga me molesta'); 'no porque' plus the subjunctive
Verbs whose meaning changes with the mood: 'decir que' (inform or order), 'sentir que' (feel or regret), 'insistir en que' (state or demand)

units.title: Ser and estar, por and para: finer distinctions
goals: Use 'ser' and 'estar' with adjectives that change meaning
Use 'ser' for where and when an event takes place
Use 'estar' for a quality perceived at the moment ('la sopa está rica')
Choose 'por' and 'para' in their less obvious uses
grammar: Adjectives that change meaning: 'ser listo' and 'estar listo', 'ser aburrido' and 'estar aburrido', 'ser rico' and 'estar rico', 'ser malo' and 'estar malo', 'ser vivo' and 'estar vivo'
'Ser' for events ('La fiesta es en mi casa'); 'estar' for a change or a perception ('¡Qué alto estás!')
'Por' and 'para' further: 'para' for a point of view and a comparison ('para mí', 'para su edad'); 'estar por', used in Mexico for 'to be about to'; 'por si acaso', 'por lo visto', 'para colmo'
Fixed expressions with 'estar': 'estar de malas', 'estar harto', 'estar de acuerdo'

units.title: Mexican speech: idioms, slang and diminutives
goals: Understand common Mexican slang and idioms
Use diminutives naturally
Recognize regional speech and words that come from Nahuatl
Judge the register of what you hear
grammar: Diminutives in '-ito', '-cito' and '-ecito', with spelling changes ('poquito', 'amiguito'), and their affective and softening uses; augmentatives in '-ote' and '-ón'
Discourse markers and slang: 'órale', 'ándale', 'híjole', '¿a poco?', '¿qué onda?', 'chido', 'padre', 'la neta', 'no manches', 'güey' and its register, 'pues' and 'este' as fillers
Idioms: 'echarle ganas', 'ponerse las pilas', 'dar el avión', 'estar en la luna'
Words from Nahuatl ('cuate', 'chapulín', 'popote', 'guajolote', 'elote', 'papalote', 'tianguis') and regional speech (the north, Yucatán, Mexico City)

units.title: Reading literature and poetry
goals: Read short public-domain literary texts by Mexican authors
Understand figurative language
Discuss a text's meaning
Recognize literary word order and verb forms
grammar: Literary word order: inversion, the adjective before the noun for emphasis, pronouns attached to a conjugated verb in older texts ('díjole')
The '-se' imperfect subjunctive, and the '-ra' form with the meaning of the pluperfect in literary texts
Figures of speech: 'la metáfora', 'el símil', 'la personificación', 'la hipérbole', 'la ironía'
Reading strategies: word families, prefixes ('des-', 'in-', 're-') and suffixes ('-dad', '-ción', '-oso', '-mente')
vocabulary_themes: Amado Nervo and Manuel Gutiérrez Nájera (public-domain poems)
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz and Ramón López Velarde (public-domain excerpts)

units.title: Formal writing and registers
goals: Write a structured essay and a formal letter
Adapt tone to context
Use connectors that hold a text together
Avoid colloquial forms in formal writing
grammar: Essay structure: introduction, development and conclusion, with connectors ('en primer lugar', 'además', 'por consiguiente', 'no obstante', 'en resumen', 'cabe señalar que')
Nominalization ('el aumento de los precios' in place of 'los precios aumentaron') and impersonal constructions in formal prose
Formal letters and emails: openings and closings, 'usted' and 'ustedes', 'le' and 'les' for the reader
Punctuation and spelling in formal texts: commas, accents on capital letters, numbers and dates

units.title: Mexico: regions, culture and history
goals: Read and discuss extended texts about Mexico
Talk about regions, festivals and traditions
Understand the major periods of Mexican history
Narrate history with the past tenses and the passive
grammar: Historical narration: preterite, imperfect, pluperfect, the historical present and the passive
Cause, consequence and chronology in written Spanish ('debido a', 'a raíz de', 'a partir de', 'a finales del siglo')
Dates, centuries and percentages in formal texts
Reading strategies for long texts: topic sentences, connectors, meaning from context
vocabulary_themes: festivals and traditions ('el Día de Muertos', 'la ofrenda')
music, crafts and food ('el mariachi', 'la artesanía')

units.title: B2 capstone: argument and nuance
goals: Argue a position with nuance
Switch registers
Combine all the tenses and moods fluently
Understand fast, natural speech
grammar: Full review of the indicative, the subjunctive, the conditional, the compound tenses and pronoun placement
Nuance: concessive and adversative structures ('aun así', 'con todo', 'por mucho que', 'si bien')
Emphasis: 'fue ... quien', 'es ... donde', 'lo que ... es', 'el que ... es'
Review of common B2 errors and advanced idiomatic usage
vocabulary_themes: abstract topics ('la identidad', 'la desigualdad', 'el desarrollo', 'la migración')
